report:
# Whole-Body Vibration Therapy and Fracture Prevention in Osteoporosis: Evidence Review

## Conclusion
The evidence is **mixed and not conclusively supportive** of your "yes" answer. While some studies suggest whole-body vibration (WBV) may improve bone mineral density (BMD) and reduce fall risk, direct evidence that it prevents fractures in osteoporosis sufferers remains limited and inconsistent.

## Key Evidence

**Supportive findings:**
- A 2022 systematic review concluded WBV "reduced fracture risk in healthy individuals without chronic illnesses" and "may be a safe and beneficial supplementary treatment for osteoporosis and help prevent fractures" — though notably, the fracture risk reduction was demonstrated in *healthy* individuals, not confirmed osteoporosis patients ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0965229922000139)).
- A BMJ Open meta-analysis found significant effects of WBV on lumbar spine BMD in adults ≥50, but BMD is a surrogate marker, not direct fracture prevention ([bmjopen.bmj.com](https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/7/12/e018342)).

**Negative/inconclusive findings:**
- One trial found "Whole body vibration has no overall treatment effect on bone mineral density, bone turnover markers... in women with postmenopausal osteoporosis" ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09638288.2016.1226417)).
- The European League Against Rheumatism found "insufficient evidence to recommend whole-body vibration for fragility fracture prevention in adults over 50 years" with bone fragility ([droracle.ai](https://www.droracle.ai/articles/633104/what-is-the-evidence-for-using-vibration-plates-as)).

## Bottom Line
WBV shows promise as a complementary approach and may improve BMD and balance, but current evidence does **not** robustly demonstrate fracture prevention in osteoporosis sufferers specifically. The answer is closer to "possibly, but not yet proven."
